opus-5.5.text:
I'd actually push back a little on the framing. Operator isn't really about the physical world. It's an agent operating inside a browser: it sees screenshots, moves a mouse, clicks, types. That's still the digital world. But I think it's an important step, because it changes what we ask the model to do. Before, the model mostly answered questions: you ask, it responds, done. With Operator, the model has to take actions in an environment, see what happens, and decide the next step over many turns. That's an agent, and that's fundamentally a reinforcement learning problem.

So when I look at Operator, what I see is OpenAI saying: we have strong reasoning models from the o-series, and now we're connecting that reasoning to actions. That's the right direction. In my view, the next big phase of AI is moving from "a model that thinks" to "a model that acts," and computer use is the natural first playground. The environment is fully digital, you can run it at scale, you can reset it, and you can collect a huge amount of interaction data. You can't do that with a physical robot.

Honestly, the current version isn't that impressive yet. It's slow, it gets stuck, it needs humans to take over for logins or payments, and on long tasks the error rate compounds. If each step is 95% reliable, after twenty steps you're in trouble. That's the classic RL problem of long-horizon decision-making, and I don't think you solve it with pretraining or supervised fine-tuning alone. You need large-scale RL in real environments, with the model trying, failing, and learning from feedback. That's also why we've been building RL infrastructure at Tsinghua and Ant, because the bottleneck is really the systems for doing agentic RL efficiently.

As for the physical world, I think the path goes through the digital world first. Robotics has a data problem and a hardware problem. The data is expensive, the environments are slow, and every embodiment is different. A digital agent like Operator lets you develop the core abilities, like planning, using feedback, recovering from mistakes, and handling long tasks, in a setting where you can iterate fast. Once those abilities are mature, transferring them to embodied systems becomes much more realistic. So I see Operator as a very early version of something important. It's not extending intelligence into the physical world yet, but it's building the agentic capability that will eventually get us there.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator is still confined to the digital world and explicitly states it is “not extending intelligence into the physical world yet.”

r002.rationale: The response says OpenAI is connecting strong reasoning models from the o-series to actions, but does not state that Operator’s pure logical reasoning is no stronger than o3’s.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd frame Operator as a meaningful step, but I'd push back a little on the phrase "physical world." What Operator actually does is take a browser and let the model see the screen, move a cursor, click buttons, fill in forms. That's intelligence extended into the digital world, into the environments humans already built for themselves. It's not touching atoms yet.

That said, I don't think that's a criticism. I actually think the browser is the right first environment, for a few reasons.

First, the web is the largest action space humans have ever created. Almost every service we use has a web interface. If a model can operate a browser reliably, it can book a flight, order groceries, compare prices, submit a form to a government website. You get enormous coverage without building any new infrastructure.

Second, and this is the part I care about most from a research perspective, it's a real test of long-horizon decision-making. Chatbots are mostly single-turn or short-turn. An agent operating a browser has to perceive, plan, act, observe the result, and recover when something goes wrong. A pop-up appears, a page doesn't load, the layout is different from what it expected. That feedback loop is essentially a reinforcement learning problem, and the web is a cheap, scalable simulator for it. You can run millions of episodes without breaking a robot arm.

So when I assess the progress, I'd say the capability is real but still early. In the demos it looks magical. In practice, on tasks that take twenty or thirty steps, the success rate drops quickly. The model gets confused, it loops, it clicks the wrong thing and doesn't notice. The hard problem isn't perception anymore, it's robustness and self-correction over long sequences. And that's exactly the thing RL is good at improving, so I'm fairly optimistic about the trajectory.

The other thing I'd say is that the lessons here transfer. The skills you need for a web agent, grounding language in an environment, verifying your own actions, knowing when to ask the human for help, are the same skills you need for an embodied agent. The difference is that in the physical world, mistakes are expensive and data is scarce. So I see Operator less as "AI entering the physical world" and more as a training ground. If we can get agents to be reliable in a browser, that's a necessary step before we can trust them with anything physical.

So my honest assessment: good direction, right environment to start with, but we're at the beginning of the reliability curve rather than the end.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator acts in a browser and is “not touching atoms yet,” describing it as a training ground before agents can be trusted with anything physical.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison between Operator’s logical reasoning and o3’s.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between acting in the digital world and acting in the physical world. Operator is a step toward AI that can do things for you, rather than just answer questions. But operating a computer and operating a robot involve very different challenges.

The connection is the decision-making loop: observe what’s happening, choose an action, see the result, and adjust. That’s an important capability for both. The question is whether the system can sustain that loop reliably when something unexpected happens, recognize a mistake, and recover.

In the physical world, the consequences are harder to reverse. You have uncertainty in sensing, constraints on movement, and interactions with people. So I’d view Operator as progress toward more general agents, but not by itself as evidence that physical-world intelligence is solved. The meaningful milestone is reliable action under uncertainty, not simply a successful demonstration.

This communicates that Operator has not yet genuinely extended intelligence into the physical world.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between acting in a digital environment and acting in the physical world. Operator is a step toward intelligence that can take actions, observe the results, and adjust, rather than just produce an answer. That interaction loop is important.

But a computer interface is still a much more constrained environment than the physical world. With a robot, you have to deal with sensing, movement, uncertainty, and consequences that may be difficult to reverse. So I would view Operator as progress toward a more general agent, while being cautious about treating it as evidence that physical intelligence is already solved.

The key question is reliability: can the system complete a long task, recognize when something has gone wrong, and recover—or ask for help? That matters in both settings, and it becomes even more important when actions affect the physical world.
